siegrist2022_sufficient_complete.title: Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, §7.6: Sufficient, Complete and Ancillary Statistics

article_lead.description: a statistic whose expectation distinguishes all its nonzero functions across a model, making unbiased estimation through it unique

new_bank_questions.title: Completeness and an unbiased pair probability
new_bank_questions.body: In three independent Bernoulli trials let T be the success count. Show that h(T)=T(T-1)/6 is unbiased for p², and evaluate it at T=2. Why is this function unique among unbiased functions of T when p ranges over (0,1)?
new_bank_questions.answer: There are six ordered pairs of distinct trials. Each pair succeeds with probability p², so E[T(T-1)/6]=p². At T=2 the estimate is 2/6=1/3. If another function of T were unbiased for p², its difference from h would have expectation zero for every p. The binomial count is complete on (0,1), so the difference is zero almost surely.

new_bank_questions.title: A sufficient count that is not complete
new_bank_questions.body: Let T count successes in two independent Bernoulli trials, but suppose the model permits only p=1/2. Find a nonzero function q(T) whose expectation is zero, and explain what changes if p can range through (0,1).
new_bank_questions.answer: Take q(T)=T-1. At the sole allowed value p=1/2, E[T]=2p=1, so E[q(T)]=0, although q(T) is -1 or 1 with positive probability. Thus T is not complete for the restricted model. If p varies through (0,1), E[q(T)]=2p-1 is not identically zero; indeed the binomial polynomial argument shows no nonzero q has zero expectation for every p in that interval.
